pythagoras.title: Right triangles, squared
pythagoras.summary: Find an unknown diagonal by turning two side lengths into square areas.
pythagoras.focus: Right angles, square areas, and the missing side

cues.text: A ladder, a wall, and the ground form a right triangle. The little square marks the ninety degree corner, where the wall meets the ground.
The two sides that touch that corner are the legs, labeled A and B. The diagonal across from it is the hypotenuse, labeled C.
A square built on each side has area side times side. The two leg squares together have the same area as the hypotenuse square. That gives us our formula.
Put the ladder three meters from the wall and reach four meters up. Three and four are the legs, so only the diagonal is unknown.
Three times three gives nine square meters. Four times four gives sixteen. Add the areas: nine plus sixteen is twenty five. That is C squared, not C.
What positive number times itself gives twenty five? Five. The ladder is five meters long. Notice that we return to ordinary length units, and five is longer than either leg.
Now both legs change: one is six and the other is eight. Start by squaring the legs. What length belongs on the diagonal?
Take a moment to work it out. You can pause here to sketch.
Six squared is thirty six; eight squared is sixty four. Their sum is one hundred. Take its positive square root to get ten, not one hundred.
Check the result: ten times ten is one hundred. And six, eight, ten is a scaled version of the earlier triangle: every side doubled, not just the diagonal.
First check for a right angle. The theorem is not a shortcut for every triangle, and the hypotenuse is not always drawn on top.
To find the hypotenuse, add the leg squares. To find a missing leg, subtract the known leg square from the hypotenuse square instead.
Finish with a square root, then check the units and side lengths. Read the class notes to work through a missing leg on your own.

notes.title: Identify the three sides first
notes.text: Find the marked 90° corner before using the formula. The two sides that meet there are the legs a and b, and the side opposite it is c. Rotate the triangle in your mind if you need to: c is identified by its position, not by which side is slanted.

notes.title: Area is not length
notes.text: For the ladder, the right triangle has legs 3 m and 4 m. A square on the first leg has area 9 m²; a square on the second has area 16 m². They add to 25 m², the area of the square built on the ladder. Taking the positive square root converts that area back to the side length, 5 m.

notes.title: Finding a leg is the same rule rearranged
notes.text: If a right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and known leg 5, the missing leg’s square is the part of 13² left over after removing 5². Subtract the square areas first, then take the positive root to obtain the length. Check that the missing leg is shorter than 13.

pythagoras.mistake: Don’t add the side lengths to find the hypotenuse, and don’t give the total area as a length. Three plus four is seven; the ladder in our example is five meters.

practice.question: A rectangular garden is 8 m wide and 15 m long. How long is the straight diagonal path from corner to corner?
practice.answer: The rectangle makes a right triangle with legs 8 m and 15 m. Square and add: 64 + 225 = 289. The positive square root is 17, so the path is 17 m long.

fractions.title: Fractions, piece by piece
fractions.summary: Use a bar model to see why fractions need equal pieces before you add them.
fractions.focus: Equal parts, equivalent fractions, and common denominators

cues.text: Start with one chocolate bar. This is our whole. Cut it into four pieces of the same size, so every piece represents one quarter.
The bottom number is the denominator: it counts all the equal pieces in one whole. The top number is the numerator: it counts the pieces we selected.
I shaded three pieces, so our fraction is three quarters. The fourth piece remains part of the whole even though it is not shaded. Count it in the denominator.
How much is one half plus one quarter? A half and a quarter are different sized pieces, so counting them together as they are would be misleading.
Compare two bars of the same length. The shaded half on the first bar ends exactly where two shaded quarters end on the second. One half is two quarters.
Now both pieces are measured in quarters. Two quarters plus one quarter makes three quarters. The denominator stays four because we added pieces, not the number of cuts in the whole.
Your turn: add three eighths and one quarter of the same bar. How many eighths cover the same length as one quarter?
Pause to draw eight equal boxes. Try it before the answer appears.
Every quarter covers two eighths, because eight pieces fit where four larger pieces used to fit. Rename one quarter as two eighths without changing its value.
Add three eighths and two eighths to get five eighths. Find the five shaded boxes on the board. We still divide the whole bar into eight.
For adding fractions, start with the same whole. Half of a small bar and half of a big bar are not equal amounts of chocolate.
Rename both fractions using equal sized pieces. Then add the top numbers only. The bottom number says how many of those pieces fit in one whole.
Finally, check the picture. Five eighths is more than half because half is four eighths. But it is still less than a whole bar.

notes.title: What the two numbers count
notes.text: The denominator is a description of the unit, not a count of what is left. A bar cut into 4 equal pieces uses quarters, whether you shade 0, 1, or 3 pieces. The numerator counts how many of that unit you have. Keep the whole the same when you compare amounts.
notes.equation: ¾ = 3 selected pieces ÷ 4 equal pieces in the whole

notes.title: Equivalent fractions rename the same amount
notes.text: Cut each half of a bar in two. You now have 4 pieces. The area that used to be called one half covers 2 of the new pieces, so it is two quarters. The amount did not grow: you divided both the shaded and unshaded pieces into smaller pieces.

notes.title: Choose a denominator both fractions can use
notes.text: For three eighths plus a quarter, choose eighths because 8 is a multiple of 4. Multiply the numerator and denominator of 1/4 by 2 to keep its value the same. Now the pieces have the same size, so add their counts. The result is one eighth past one half.

fractions.mistake: Do not add the denominators. One half plus one quarter is not two sixths. Two sixths would be less than one half, but adding a positive quarter must make the amount larger.

practice.question: You use one third of a meter of ribbon for a bow and one sixth for a tag. How much ribbon do you use altogether?
practice.answer: A third is two sixths: multiply both numbers of 1/3 by 2. Add 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 of a meter. Simplify 3/6 by dividing both numbers by 3: you used one half of a meter.

human-cell.title: Inside the Human Cell
human-cell.summary: Explore the microscopic anatomy of an animal cell, including the nucleus, mitochondria, and cell membrane.
human-cell.focus: Cell membrane, nucleus, mitochondria (ATP), endoplasmic reticulum, and ribosomes.

cues.text: Every human cell is completely enclosed by a flexible cell membrane. This lipid bilayer controls which essential nutrients enter and which waste products leave the cellular interior.
Inside lies the cytoplasm, a rich water-based jelly filling the entire interior cell space. Cellular organelles float safely in the cytoplasm, suspended and organized by fibrous protein structures.
Notice the circular animal cell shape on our board: flexible and dynamic, unlike rigid plant cells with stiff cellulose cell walls and green chloroplasts.
At the center sits the nucleus, the master control center of the entire cell. It securely houses our DNA genetic instructions inside a protective double membrane equipped with nuclear pores.
Surrounding the nucleus are oval mitochondria, often called the powerhouses of the cell. Mitochondria use oxygen and glucose from food to generate chemical energy in the form of ATP.
The inner folded membrane of each mitochondrion, called cristae, creates vast surface area for chemical reactions. Active cells like muscle cells contain thousands of energetic mitochondria.
Look at the ribbon-like folded channels around the nucleus dotted with tiny dark specks. Which cellular organelle manufactures new proteins directly from genetic codes?
Pause here to trace the folded membranes. Think about how ribosomes and ER cooperate.
Those tiny specks are ribosomes, and the folded highway is the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Ribosomes read RNA copies from the nucleus and assemble chains of amino acids into proteins.
The Golgi apparatus then packages these finished proteins into vesicles for delivery throughout your body. Check: ribosomes build, the Golgi packages and ships.
All vital organelle systems work together in wonderful harmony: the nucleus instructs, mitochondria power, ribosomes build, and the flexible cell membrane protects.
Trillions of human cells specialize into nerve, muscle, bone, and skin cells while sharing these same fundamental organelle components.
Read the study notes to compare animal and plant cell structures, and ask your tutor any question about cellular respiration or protein synthesis.

notes.title: The nucleus commands and protects DNA
notes.text: The nucleus is enclosed by a double-layered nuclear envelope with pores regulating transport. Inside, DNA stores the master genetic blueprint for synthesizing all proteins required by the human body.

notes.title: Mitochondria generate cellular fuel
notes.text: Through cellular respiration, mitochondria break down glucose in the presence of oxygen to synthesize adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the primary energy currency utilized across all cellular metabolic processes.

notes.title: Protein production pipeline: Ribosomes to Golgi
notes.text: Ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum assemble amino acid chains. The synthesized proteins travel to the Golgi apparatus, where they undergo folding, biochemical modification, and vesicular packaging.

human-cell.mistake: Don’t confuse animal cells with plant cells. Human animal cells possess flexible cell membranes and mitochondria, but do not contain rigid cellulose cell walls, large central vacuoles, or chloroplasts.

practice.question: Why do active muscle cells contain substantially higher concentrations of mitochondria than skin cells?
practice.answer: Muscle cells continuously contract and require high quantities of ATP energy, which mitochondria produce via aerobic cellular respiration to power muscular exertion.

heart-diagram.title: Human Heart & Double Circulation
heart-diagram.summary: Follow oxygen-poor and oxygen-rich blood through the heart's four chambers, valves, and vessels.
heart-diagram.focus: Chambers, heart valves, and pulmonary vs systemic circulation

cues.text: The human heart is a powerful double pump about the size of a clenched fist. Look at the cross-section diagram on our whiteboard: the anatomical right side is shown in blue, and the left side in red.
The two upper receiving chambers are the atria: the right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body, while the left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.
Below them sit the muscular pumping ventricles. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, while the thicker left ventricle propels oxygenated blood to the entire body.
Oxygen-depleted blood from our upper and lower body returns through the superior and inferior vena cava veins directly into the right atrium.
When the right atrium contracts, blood flows across the three-flapped tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The tricuspid valve snaps shut during contraction to prevent backward leakage.
The right ventricle then contracts, pumping blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary artery toward both lungs. Notice that this is the only human artery carrying deoxygenated blood.
Inside the lungs, red blood cells drop off carbon dioxide waste and absorb fresh oxygen. Four pulmonary veins return this bright red blood into the left atrium.
Take a moment to inspect the left side of the heart. Which valve guards the entrance to the left ventricle?
Blood passes through the two-flapped bicuspid, or mitral, valve into the left ventricle. Notice the thick muscular wall: it must generate high arterial pressure to reach every organ from head to toe.
Contraction forces blood past the aortic valve and into the massive arched aorta. From here, high-pressure oxygenated blood cascades through branching arteries to fuel our body.
Human circulation operates as two connected loops: the low-pressure pulmonary circuit to the lungs, and the high-pressure systemic circuit to the body.
The muscular interventricular septum down the center completely separates both sides, ensuring deoxygenated and oxygenated blood never mix.
Read the study notes to review valve timing and cardiac output, and ask your tutor to highlight or circle any structure on the diagram.

notes.title: Pulmonary Circuit (Right Heart to Lungs)
notes.text: Deoxygenated systemic blood arrives through the superior and inferior vena cava into the right atrium, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and is pumped via the pulmonary trunk to the lungs for gas exchange.
notes.equation: Vena Cava → Right Atrium → Tricuspid → Right Ventricle → Pulmonary Artery → Lungs

notes.title: Systemic Circuit (Left Heart to Body)
notes.text: Oxygenated blood returns via four pulmonary veins into the left atrium, passes through the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the thick-walled left ventricle, and is ejected through the aortic valve into the aorta at systemic pressure.
notes.equation: Pulmonary Veins → Left Atrium → Bicuspid → Left Ventricle → Aorta → Body

notes.title: Unidirectional Flow: Heart Valves
notes.text: Four valves maintain strictly one-way blood flow: atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and bicuspid) close during ventricular systole to produce the 'lub' sound, while semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) close during diastole to produce the 'dub' sound.
notes.equation: Systole: AV valves close (lub) · Diastole: Semilunar valves close (dub)

heart-diagram.mistake: Don’t assume all arteries carry oxygenated blood and all veins carry deoxygenated blood. Arteries are defined as vessels carrying blood AWAY from the heart, so the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the right ventricle. Veins carry blood TOWARD the heart, so pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood.

practice.question: Why is the myocardial wall of the left ventricle significantly thicker than that of the right ventricle?
practice.answer: The right ventricle only needs to pump blood a short distance to the low-resistance lungs (pulmonary circuit), whereas the left ventricle must generate enough systemic pressure to propel blood throughout the entire body (systemic circuit).
